list.listitem: Calculate and plot body mass index (BMI) at all well child visits. C
Obesity in children and adolescents is defined as having a BMI at the 95th percentile or higher, and overweight is defined as having a BMI between the 85th and 94th percentile for age and sex. C

If BMI for age and sex is at the 85th to 94th percentile with no risk factors, obtain a fasting lipid profile. If risk factors are present or if BMI for age and sex is at the 95th percentile or higher, additionally obtain AST, ALT, and fasting glucose. C
Provide 5-2-1-0 counseling for all patients (≥5 servings of fruits and vegetables, ≤2 hours of screen time, ≥1 hour of physical activity, and 0 sugar-sweetened beverages). C
The patient advances through the four stages of treatment depending on age and BMI (see and ). C

background.definition: Obesity in children and adolescents 2 to 8 years of age is defined as having a BMI at the 95th percentile or higher for age and sex. Overweight is defined as BMI at the 85th percentile or higher but less than 95th percentile for age and sex.

list.listitem: Prevalence has doubled among 6- to 11-year-olds and tripled among 12- to 17-year-olds between 1976 to 1980 and 1999 to 2002.

Currently 17% of children and adolescents in the United States are obese. 4% to 6% of all youth in the United States are severely obese, with a BMI ≥99%, BMI ≥120% of the 95th percentile, or BMI ≥35 kg/m2.
Prevalence is highest among African-American, Latino, and Native American children and adolescents.

Obese children and adolescents are more likely to be obese adults. The total cost of obesity is estimated to be approximately $117 billion a year. Direct health care costs make up more than half of this total cost.
Obesity is the most common nutritional disease of children and adolescents living in the United States.
Obese children and adolescents have lower quality of life compared with those who are nonobese.
Excessive caloric intake, large portion sizes, and consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages (RR 1.6; 95% CI 1.1-2.2).
Skipping breakfast.
Low consumption of fruits and vegetables.
Restaurant/fast food consumption.
Increased sedentary activities (ie, excessive screen time) and decreased physical activity.
Cultural beliefs.
Genetic factors (ie, family history of obesity).
Poverty, food insecurity, and lack of access to healthy foods.
Lack of safe play spaces and resources for physical activity.
There were no significant differences in obesity at 3 to 7 years of age between offspring of mothers treated for GDM and offspring of mothers without GDM.

Critical periods that contribute to the development of obesity include: (1) prenatal period: maternal diet, maternal gestational diabetes; (2) infancy: low birth weight, absence of breastfeeding; (3) preschool period: early adiposity rebound; and (4) adolescence: decline in physical activity, unhealthy food behaviors.
Obesity is a complex disorder with psychosocial, cultural, genetic, metabolic, and biochemical factors playing a role in its pathophysiology.
There is fair evidence for use of BMI as a screening tool to identify 2- to 18-year-olds who are obese or overweight. Screen for obesity in children 6 and older using BMI. C

BMI correlates well with percent body fat and skinfold thickness measurements in children and adolescents, and increased BMI is associated with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and reduced life expectancy. BMI may not accurately reflect percent body fat in very muscular patients. C
See for lifestyle recommendations to prevent hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes in obese children and adolescents. C

The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that providing or referring children and adolescents, 6 years or older, with a high BMI (at least 95th percentile for age and sex) to comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions has a moderate net benefit (B recommendation). Although the mean reduction in BMI with intervention was small (-0.7 compared with control), larger benefits occurred with more contact hours (> 26 total hours) that also offered physical activity sessions.C

Obesity is defined as having a BMI at the 95th percentile or higher, and overweight is defined as having a BMI at the 85th percentile or higher for age and sex in a 2- to 18-year-old child or adolescent. C
Assess diet, level of physical activity, and sedentary behaviors, as well as parent and child self-efficacy and readiness to change in all patients. C
Obtain a focused family history of obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and early deaths from heart disease/stroke. C

If BMI for age and sex is at the 85th to 94th percentile with no risk factors, obtain a fasting lipid profile. If risk factors are present or if BMI for age and sex is higher than the 95th percentile, additionally obtain AST, ALT, and fasting glucose. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Fatigue, cold sensitivity, constipation, pale and dry skin, muscle weakness

Retinitis pigmentosa, polydactyly, short stature, developmental delay
Tall stature, rapid bone age advancement

list.listitem: Overweight is defined as BMI at the 85th to less than 95th percentile for age and sex.
Obesity is defined as BMI at the 95th percentile or higher for age and sex.

Assess readiness to change based on five stages of change: Precontemplation (patient not considering change), Contemplation (patient evaluating reasons for and against the change), Preparation (patient planning for the change), Action (patient has made the change within the last 6 months), and Maintenance (patient has maintained the change for more than 6 months).

Assess patient and caregiver motivation using: the Importance Ruler (on a scale of 1-10, how important is the behavior change to the patient and caregiver?) and the Confidence Ruler (on a scale of 1-10, how confident do the patient and caregiver feel in their ability to make the change?).
The Weight, Activity, Variety, and Excess (WAVE) tool has been shown to be a feasible, acceptable, and quick method of assessing weight and weight-related behavioral risk factors.
Behavioral risk factor assessment can additionally include screening for unhealthy eating behaviors (sneaking food, hoarding, binge eating, purging, skipping meals).
Past medical history: Birth weight, maternal gestational diabetes, duration of breastfeeding, chronic medications, developmental delay.
Social history: Family stressors, school performance, teasing, bullying.
Family history: Obesity, hypertension, heart disease, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, thyroid disease, depression.

Review of systems: Symptoms suggesting sleep apnea (snoring, apnea, daytime somnolence), asthma (cough, exercise intolerance), gastroesophageal reflux disease [GERD], musculoskeletal problems like Blount's disease or slipped capital femoral epiphysis (limb/joint pain), irregular or heavy menses, pseudotumor cerebri (headaches), gallbladder disease (right upper quadrant pain), depression or other emotional problems.
Physical examination: Blood pressure, acanthosis nigricans, striae, hirsutism, thyroid enlargement.
Calculate and plot the BMI at least once a year in all children and adolescents.
Fasting lipid profile: Order if BMI is at the 85th percentile or higher.

Fasting blood glucose: Order if BMI is at the 85th to 94th percentile with risk factors (eg, family history of obesity-related comorbidities, elevated blood pressure, elevated lipid levels, or tobacco use) OR if BMI is at the 95th percentile or higher.
AST and ALT: Order if BMI is at the 85th percentile or higher with risk factors OR BMI is at the 95th percentile or higher.
Measure growth parameters and plot them in regard to age and sex in all children at every well child visit.
Calculate the BMI and plot it in regard to age and sex in all children older than 2 years at every well child visit.

outlines the four stages of overweight and obesity management: Stage 1, Prevention Plus; Stage 2, Structured Weight Management; Stage 3, Comprehensive Multidisciplinary Protocol; Stage 4, Tertiary Care Referral. C

Behavioral and lifestyle interventions result in better weight management than standard care or self-help interventions, based on meta-analysis of limited clinical trial data. B Educational interventions also improve BMI. A
The patient advances through each stage depending on age and BMI (). C

Medications alone are not effective in treating obesity, and data on their long-term effect on growth and development in children are not available. Medications combined with structured lifestyle modification result in only modest weight loss of 5% to 10%, which usually plateaus in 4 to 6 months, with possibility of weight regain.

Sibutramine, in combination with a behavioral treatment program, may be beneficial in reducing weight and metabolic risk factors in obese adolescents 16 years or older. More research is needed to determine its safety and efficacy for long-term use in adolescents.
Orlistat in combination with diet and physical activity changes may result in weight reduction in adolescents 12 years or older.
A limited systematic review found that when added to diet and exercise, metformin has minimal effect on BMI in children.

Semaglutide, in combination with lifestyle interventions, may increase weight loss in obese adolescents compared to lifestyle interventions alone (percent change in BMI -16.1% vs +0.6%, P < .001). However, semaglutide was associated with an increase in gastrointestinal complaints.
In children aged 6 to 11 years with obesity, liraglutide reduced BMI by 7.4% more than placebo at 1 year (−5.8% vs +1.6%, 95% CI −11.6% to −3.2%).

Obese children and adolescents randomized to weekly injections of tirzepatide, independent of dose, experienced greater improvements in glycemic control than those who received a placebo. Additionally, the participants treated with tirzepatide experienced greater dose-dependent weight loss than those treated with a placebo (9.3% vs 0.4%).

Bariatric surgery may be indicated for morbidly obese adolescents with life-threatening comorbidities of obesity who do not respond to intensive nonsurgical treatment. Surgical critieria include: (1) minimum of 6 months of lifestyle modifications, (2) physiologic maturity, (3) adequate decision-making capacity, (4) BMI greater than 40 with severe obesity-related comorbidities or BMI greater than 50 with some less severe obesity-related comorbidities, and (5) agreement to avoid pregnancy for at least 1 year after surgery.

No data are available to demonstrate that surgical weight loss in adolescents reduces early mortality. There are no data on the comparative safety and efficacy of various surgical weight loss procedures in adolescents.

Early complications of bariatric surgery in adolescents include pulmonary embolism, wound infection, and stomal stenoses. Late complications of bariatric surgery in adolescents, reported in up to 15% of patients, include pulmonary embolism, small-bowel obstruction, incisional hernias, and late weight regain.
The efficacy and safety of adjustable gastric banding for adolescents are being investigated in the United States.
Involve the child and family in treatment. Encourage and empathize; do not criticize.
Assess stage of readiness to change and match counseling accordingly. Help patient and family set one to two achievable individualized goals, and negotiate small incremental steps.
Review goals at frequent follow-up visits to facilitate accountability, with self-monitoring of diet and activity.

Implement positive feedback by the health care provider and parents, with use of nonfood rewards for positive diet and physical activity behaviors, preferably rewards promoting family interaction. Emphasize problem-solving skills with respect to lifestyle behavior and relapse.
A randomized trial motivational interviewing versus usual care in primary care pediatric practices found an increase in BMI in the intervention group.
Family counseling may be indicated if stress or psychosocial problems interfere with treatment.

A Cochrane review found that child obesity prevention programs in children 6 to 12 years of age decreased BMI, including school curricula that include healthy eating, physical activity and body image; increased physical activity throughout the school week; improved nutritional quality of food served in schools; environment and cultural support for eating healthier foods and being active throughout the day; support for teachers and staff to implement health promotion strategies; and parent support and home activities to encourage children to be more active, eat more nutritious foods, and have less screen time.

A meta-analysis found that merely calculating BMI and brief counseling in primary care practices did not reduce BMI. A randomized controlled study of 1369 infants found that intensive motivational interviewing and counseling of parents of 9- to 10-month-old infants (1 group session, 6 individual sessions, and 2 individual telephone sessions with counseling on healthy food choices and physical activity) had no effect on the child or mother's BMI, waist circumference, likelihood of being overweight, or physical activity 3 years later (when child was 4 years old).

A randomized clinical trial showed that patients receiving a digital intervention consisting of interactive text messaging, a web-based dashboard, and clinic-based healthy behavior counseling had lower rates of child obesity compared to children who received counseling alone (12.7% vs 7.4%, NNT=20).
Decrease caloric intake and portion size, frequency of eating out at restaurants and fast food establishments, and sugar-sweetened beverage consumption.
Consume breakfast daily.

Increase physical activity and include physical activity in the daily routine (eg, walking, biking, household chores). Using a pedometer to measure steps walked, distance walked, and energy expended is associated with significant increases in physical activity and significant decreases in BMI.
Decrease sedentary activities: limit screen time to less than 2 hours a day.
Obese children and adolescents have increased risk of becoming obese as adults, with a 20% probability if obese at age 4 and 80% probability if obese during adolescence. B

Obese children and adolescents face increased risks of developing hypertension, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea, steatohepatitis, gallbladder diseases, orthopedic problems, and psychosocial issues. B
Ten years after behavioral family-based treatment for childhood obesity, 34% of patients decreased their percentage of overweight by 20% or more, and 30% of patients were no longer obese. B
Important factors enabling successful weight loss include having parents actively participate in the treatment plan, as well as combining dietary changes with physical activity. B

feature.caption: Staged Treatment of Pediatric Obesity.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Treatment Specifics
1. Prevention Plus (5-2-1-0) counseling ≥5 servings of fruits and vegetables ≤2 hours of screen time ≥1 hour of physical activity 0 sugar-sweetened beverages
2. Structured Weight Management Above plus: Reduce energy-dense foods Structured meals ≤1 hour of screen time Diet and activity monitoring for 3 to 6 months Monthly office visits Additional support by dietician, counselor, or exercise therapist as needed
3. Comprehensive Multidisciplinary Intervention Above plus referral to multidisciplinary obesity care team and behavioral modification
4. Tertiary Care Intervention Above plus referral to pediatric tertiary weight management center.
Data from Barlow SE; Expert Committee. Expert committee recommendations regarding the prevention, assessment, and treatment of child and adolescent overweight and obesity: summary report. Pediatrics 2007;120(Suppl 4):S164–S192.
